'''''Brassia''''' is a [[genus]] of [[orchid]]s  classified in the subtribe [[Oncidiinae]]. It is native to [[Mexico]], [[Central America]], the [[West Indies]], and northern [[South America]], with one species (''B. caudata'') extending into [[Florida]].<ref name=POWO_329118-2/><ref>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=242101433 Flora of North America v 26 p 646, ''Brassia caudata'' ]</ref>

The genus was named after [[William Brass (botanist)|William Brass]], a British botanist and illustrator, who collected plants in Africa under the supervision of Sir [[Joseph Banks]]. Its abbreviation in the horticultural trade is '''Brs'''.<ref>{{cite web|title=My Huge List of Orchid Abbreviations|url=http://www.orchidsplus.com/orchid-abbreviations/|website=orchidsplus.com|date=13 June 2014 }}</ref>

== Description ==
''Brassia'' [[species]] and its popular [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrids]] are common in cultivation, and are notable for the characteristic long and spreading [[tepal]]s (in some clones longer than 50 cm), which lend them the common name '''spider orchid'''.

This [[epiphyte|epiphytic]] genus occurs in wet forests from sea level to altitudes under 1500 m, with the Peruvian [[Andes]] as its center of diversity. Occurrence is mostly restricted to a certain area, but ''Brassia caudata'' can be found over the whole geographic area.

They have large elliptic-oblong [[pseudobulb]]s with one or two leaves at the apex, lateral, unbranched  many-flowered [[inflorescence]]s with small floral [[bract]]s. The [[Labellum (botany)|lip]] is not attached to the column. The [[pollinarium]] shows a narrow stipe. There are two distichous, foliaceous [[Leaf sheath|sheaths]] around the base, from which the inflorescence emerges.

''Brassia'' has a very specific method for pollination; it uses entomophily - [[pollination]] by insects - and in this case specifically by female [[Spider wasp|spider-hunter wasps]] of the genera ''[[Pepsis]]'' and ''[[Campsomeris]]''. Mistaken by the [[mimicry]] of ''Brassia'', the wasp stings the [[Labellum (botany)|lip]], while trying to grasp its prey without any success. By these movements the wasp comes into contact with the pollinarium, that then sticks to its head. By flying to another ''Brassia'' flower, this flower gets pollinated.
